title: Designing a schema that will not hurt later
summary: The choices that are cheap today and expensive in a year: column types, storing each fact once, database rules, timestamps and soft delete.
youWillLearn: Why the schema is the hardest part of an app to change later
Which data type to pick for dates, money, ids and loose extras
What normalization means: store each fact once
How created_at, updated_at and soft delete save you, and where soft delete bites

glossary.app server: A computer, somewhere else, that runs the app's own code. Notely's runs on Vercel.
glossary.schema: The shape of your data: which tables exist, their columns, types and rules.
glossary.data type: The kind of value a column accepts, like text, integer, boolean or timestamptz.
glossary.timestamptz: Postgres type for an exact moment in time. It stores the instant in UTC and shows it in any time zone.
glossary.jsonb: Postgres type for a JSON document (nested labels and values) stored in one column. Searchable, but the shape inside is not checked unless you add rules.
glossary.normalization: Designing tables so each fact is stored in exactly one place, and everything else points to it.
glossary.constraint: A rule declared on a column or table, like not null or check, that the database enforces on every write.
glossary.default: The value a column gets when an insert does not provide one, like now() or false.
glossary.trigger: A small function the database runs on its own when a row is inserted, updated or deleted.
glossary.soft delete: Marking a row as deleted, usually with a deleted_at time, instead of removing it from the table.

steps.title: Notely's first notes table
body: Let's rewind to Notely's very first version. The app server (the computer running Notely's code) saves each note as a row in one table, notes, inside the database.
Each row holds a title, the text, a date, and the author's email. It was built in a hurry, and on day one everything works.

scene.caption: The app server saves every note into one notes table.

steps.title: Months later, three shortcuts bite
body: Each row copies the author's email, so when Maya changed hers, 300 notes kept the old one. Dates are stored as text, so '9/1/26' sorts after '10/1/26', and junk like 'soon' slips in.
And deleting a note removes it for good. Maya deleted one by mistake and wants it back. Nothing can bring it back.
changes: ~ notes: three shortcuts, three problems
~ Stale emails 0 → 300
~ Bad saves 0 → 25 a day
~ Notes lost 0 → 1

scene.caption: Three quick choices in version 1, three problems a few months later.

steps.title: A schema is a promise you keep for years
body: The schema is the shape of your data: tables, columns, types and rules. Every screen, server route and AI prompt in Notely leans on it.
Code is cheap to change. A table with a million rows is not: every change becomes a careful operation on live data (next lesson). An hour of design now saves weeks later.

callout.text: Plumbing in a new house. Moving a pipe before the walls go up takes minutes. After the family moves in, it means opening walls.

changes: ~ notes: a million rows deep, and growing

scene.caption: Rows pile up. The table's shape gets harder to change every week.

steps.title: Pick the type that matches the fact
body: Every column has a data type, and the right one works for you: dates sort as dates, numbers add up, bad values are refused.
Good defaults: text for words, bigint or uuid for ids, boolean for yes/no, numeric for money, timestamptz for moments, jsonb for loose extras like AI settings.

code.code:
create table notes (
  id bigint generated always as identity primary key,
  title text not null,
  pinned boolean not null default false,
  word_count integer,
  ai_meta jsonb,
  created_at timestamptz not null default now()
);

callout.text: Never store money in a floating-point column. Floats cannot hold most decimals exactly, so totals drift by fractions of a cent. Use numeric, or whole cents in an integer.

changes: ~ App Server → notes: a text date like 'soon' is refused
~ Bad saves 25 → 9 a day

scene.caption: A text value aimed at a timestamp column is refused at the door.

steps.title: Store each fact once
body: Maya's email was copied onto each of her notes, so changing it left 300 stale copies.

Normalization means each fact lives in one place. The email lives once, in a users table. Notes point to their owner with user_id, as in lesson 1. Change the email once, and every screen sees the new value.

callout.text: Copying on purpose is fine when you mean a snapshot. An order keeps the price that was paid, because a later price change should not rewrite old receipts. Ask: should this copy change when the original changes?

changes: + users: one row per person, the email stored once
~ notes keep only a user_id pointing at users
~ Stale emails 300 → 0

scene.caption: The email moves to users. Notes only keep a pointer.

steps.title: Let the database say no
body: Your app code will have bugs. The database is the last line of defense, so put the rules there as constraints.
not null: must be filled. unique: no repeats. check: must pass a test. references: must point at a real row. A default fills in a value when the app leaves one out.

code.code:
title   text not null check (length(title) <= 200),
pinned  boolean not null default false,
user_id bigint not null references users (id)

changes: ~ App Server → notes: a note with no title is refused
~ Bad saves 9 → 0 a day

scene.caption: A note with no title breaks a rule, so Postgres refuses it.

steps.title: Timestamps on every table
body: Give almost every table two columns: created_at, filled by default now(), and updated_at, when the row last changed. Use timestamptz, so Maya in Lisbon and Leo in Tokyo each see their own local time.
updated_at does not update itself. A trigger, a tiny function Postgres runs on its own, stamps it on every change.
changes: + Trigger: a tiny function Postgres runs on every update
~ App Server → notes: saves go through again

scene.caption: On every update, the trigger stamps updated_at before the row is saved.

steps.title: Soft delete: a trash can, not a shredder
body: Instead of removing a row, set a deleted_at time. The note leaves Maya's list but stays in the table, visible in a Trash view. That is a soft delete.
Now Undo is one update away. Normal queries add where deleted_at is null, and a scheduled job can empty old trash for good.
changes: + Trash: deleted notes, still in the table, ready for Undo
~ Trigger steps back
~ Notes lost 1 → 0

scene.caption: Deleting only stamps deleted_at. The note moves to the trash view, not out of the table.

steps.title: Where soft delete bites
body: Forget deleted_at is null in one query and trashed notes come back: in search, in exports, in the weekly summary Notely asks the Claude API (Anthropic's AI) to write.
Sometimes deleting must be real, too. When a user asks you to erase their data, as privacy laws like GDPR allow, a soft delete is not enough.

callout.text: A view such as active_notes that filters out trashed rows gives every query one safe place to read from. A trashed row still holds its unique values; a partial index (create unique index … where deleted_at is null) ignores it.

changes: + Claude API: the AI that writes Maya's weekly summary
~ Trash: its notes leak into the summary

scene.caption: One forgotten filter, and trashed notes leak into the AI summary.

steps.title: Notely's notes table, version 2
body: The schema outlives your code, so design it on purpose. Right types, each fact once, rules in the database, timestamptz timestamps, and soft delete filtered everywhere.
This is a table you could ship to a paying client, and what to ask for when Claude Code designs one.

code.code:
create table notes (
  id bigint generated always as identity primary key,
  user_id bigint not null references users (id),
  title text not null check (length(title) <= 200),
  body text not null default '',
  pinned boolean not null default false,
  created_at timestamptz not null default now(),
  updated_at timestamptz not null default now(),
  deleted_at timestamptz
);

callout.text: Check every table Claude Code proposes: times as timestamptz, money never as a float, required columns not null, real foreign keys. Is any fact stored twice? If it soft-deletes, does every query filter on deleted_at?

changes: ~ notes: version 2, typed, ruled and safe to delete from
~ Summary query filters the trash: Claude API sees live notes only

scene.caption: Version 2: typed, constrained, timestamped and safe to delete from.

quiz.question: Notely adds reminders: each one stores when it should fire. Maya is in Lisbon, Leo in Tokyo. Which column type do you pick?

options.why: Text sorts as letters, not times, and accepts anything, including typos. There is also no time zone.
It stores a wall-clock time with no zone, so 10:00 is ambiguous once users or servers sit in different zones.
It records the exact instant, sorts correctly, and shows the right local time for each person.

quiz.question: A shares table copies the recipient's email onto every shared note. A user changes their email, and share alerts keep going to the old one. What is the fix?

options.text: Keep the email once in users, and give shares a user_id pointing to it.
options.why: Normalization: the email is one fact, stored once. Change it there and every share sees the new address.

options.text: A script that updates the email on every past share when it changes.
options.why: It patches the symptom. Any code path that forgets to run it brings the bug back.

options.text: Store the email in a jsonb column instead.
options.why: The type is not the problem. The fact is still copied onto every share.

quiz.question: Notely now soft-deletes notes. Maya says a deleted note still shows up in the AI summary of her week. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Soft delete does not work with AI features.
options.why: Soft delete is only a column. The AI sees whatever rows the query hands it.

options.text: The summary's query does not filter where deleted_at is null.
options.why: Soft-deleted rows are still in the table. Every query, including ones that feed the AI, must filter them out.

options.text: The note was hard-deleted, and the AI remembered it.
options.why: The model does not remember Notely's data between calls. It only sees what the query sends it.

takeaways: The schema outlives your code. Changing it later means operating on live data.
Pick the type that matches the fact: timestamptz for times, numeric or integer cents for money, boolean for yes/no.
Normalize: store each fact once and point to it. Copy only when you mean a snapshot.
Put rules in the database: not null, unique, check, references.
Soft delete with deleted_at gives you undo, but every query must filter it, and real erasure must still be possible.
